title: What Have Ofsted Wanted Schools to Improve So Far This Year? prove-so-far-this-year/
author: Pete Foster
summary: Continuing his annual practice of analysing Ofsted reports, Pete Foster reviews roughly twenty secondary-school inspection reports from the current academic year to identify patterns in what inspectors are asking schools to improve, this time against the backdrop of a new Chief Inspector and the removal of headline one-word judgements. His conclusion is that despite the structural change, the substance of what Ofsted flags has stayed remarkably consistent: attendance (especially disparities between groups), SEND provision, and checking for understanding remain the dominant recurring themes across grade categories. He notes some newer or more frequent flags this year, including oracy (insufficient opportunity for pupils to process ideas through talk), trusts being directed to support struggling schools, and PSHE staff training gaps. The bulk of the post is a detailed, categorised breakdown of specific 'areas for development' language pulled directly from real reports, organised by overall judgement band from Outstanding/Good down to Inadequate, giving school leaders a practical reference for anticipating likely inspection feedback.
points: Foster's headline finding -- that removing one-word judgements barely changed the substance of what inspectors flag -- is a data point against the idea that structural reporting changes alone drive different inspection behaviour.

Attendance, SEND, and 'checking for understanding' emerge as the three dominant themes across nearly all judgement bands, giving school leaders a short, evidence-based priority list for pre-inspection preparation.

The newer flags he identifies this year -- oracy, trusts being directed to support schools, and PSHE staff training gaps -- suggest emerging inspection priorities worth monitoring even though they're not yet as dominant as the core three.

By organising real report language by judgement band (Outstanding/Good through Inadequate), Foster turns a full year of Ofsted reports into a practical diagnostic tool rather than a one-off commentary piece.
quotes: I find the last bit of the report with the bullet points about areas for development the most interesting because, as a school leader, I like to think through the potential pitfalls of an inspection before it happens.

Usually, I do this process at the end of the year but, with a new Chief Inspector and the removal of one-word judgements, I wanted to see if I could notice anything dramatically different about the process. The short answer is no, I couldn't.
Attendance is still one of the biggest areas across categories.
Check for understanding in various guises is the main teaching and learning focus. Do staff know what students know and adapt teaching accordingly?
Oracy was mentioned a couple of times, where schools were not providing enough opportunity for pupils to process ideas through talk.
In all, the shift to removing the single word judgements has done little to the contents of the reports (yet). I don’t think this is surprising.
